Primary high-level attack paths we consider for hosted inference: 1) sidecar/process compromise leading to exfiltration of KV cache or local model state; 2) cross-tenant inference requests attempting to influence outputs or access context of other tenants via shared caches or improper routing; 3) malicious tool/function-calls or connector abuse which cause egress to attacker-controlled hosts; 4) control-plane injection (configuration/rollout) causing model replacement or degraded controls. Compensating controls: strict tenant-level network fencing, mTLS between components, prefix/KV caching encryption + rotation, per-tenant egress allowlists with enforced DNS & IP controls, runtime kernel hardening and policy-based request routing with canaries and rollbacks.

Stephanie / team — draft threat-model and controls below. I'll attach the CSV and a short appendix with references to our runtime design doc.

Summary (one page):
- Threat vector: Sidecar compromise (attacker obtains process-level access to the per-tenant sidecar).
  Impact: potential read of in-flight prompt history and cached KV entries; possible outbound egress to attacker endpoints.
  Controls: sidecar runs in ephemeral sandbox with constrained kernel namespaces; egress only via tenant-specific egress proxy that enforces TLS termination and outbound allowlist; sidecar mount is read-only for model artifacts and KV cache encrypted at rest with tenant-specific keys; runtime enforces request-scoped capability tokens with short TTL; telemetry and hprof snapshots disabled by default; automated detection: anomaly detection for unusual outbound connections + immediate circuit-breaker.

- Threat vector: KV cache leakage via shared memory or mis-routed cache entries.
  Impact: cross-tenant leakage of recent prompts leading to data exposure.
  Controls: per-tenant KV namespaces with enforced ACLs; cache sealing: every cache item encrypted with per-tenant AEAD key, keys rotated nightly; strict serialization and length checks on cache retrievals; access logging with signed provenance.

- Threat vector: control-plane configuration injection (malicious rollout).
  Impact: model swap or policy relaxations at scale.
  Controls: rollouts require multi-person approval for production; signed rollout manifests with replay-protection; immutable audit trail (write-once logs) + enforced canary policy: traffic is routed gradually and monitored for regressions, automatic rollback on metric thresholds.

Evidence we can provide: architecture diagram (attached), signed excerpt of our rollout manifest template, sample audit log export (redacted), egress allowlist policy example.

I'll attach mitigation-matrix.csv and a short appendix (links to runtime design). Happy to tighten wording for customer.

— Rishi

Highlights (TL;DR):
- Tenant isolation: per-tenant VPCs or namespaces, enforced at the orchestration layer. Inter-tenant traffic blocked by default.
- Egress control: all outbound traffic from runtime nodes flows through tenant-scoped egress proxies with allowlists; DNS resolution governed at the proxy to prevent covert channels.
- Cache protection: KV/prefix caches encrypted with tenant-specific keys (AEAD), keys rotated nightly and access-logged.
- Sidecar hardening: sandboxed sidecars with constrained capabilities, no privileged mounts, ephemeral lifecycles, and enforced network egress via the proxy.
- Control-plane safety: signed manifests, multi-approver rollouts, canary policies and automatic rollback on anomaly detection.
